utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone after this long weekend, both in the courtroom and just outside the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Looking to the Prosecution, did I understand well that it has been arranged that the Prosecution witness Mr. Harding would be called in order to continue being cross-examined by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That's so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If there's nothing else to be discussed at this moment, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. I have just a small announcement with respect to the order of witnesses. There is a slight change to the schedule which has been filed, the date of the schedule which we had filed on 26 March, 2002. And the new order which will be formally handed over to you, I think by the end of today, will be, as we know, first it's Mr. Harding, the end of cross-examination, and then some re-examination; then, and that corresponds to the letter of 26th of March, will be Mr. Jusufovic. Then the next witness will be Ismet Fazlic. So he comes a little bit earlier. Then the next witness will be Nedim Gavranovic, then Omer Hadziabdic, and then Edin Suljic. So that means that witness Rasema Menzilovic will be moved to the week of 8th and 12th April. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your information, Mr. Waespi. Mr. Usher, may I then ask you to escort Mr. Harding into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Harding. It has been quite some time ago that you were here, and that unfortunately we had to interrupt your examination as a witness. May I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you made at the beginning of giving your testimony. And it's now up to the Defence to continue the cross-examination. Perhaps there may be re-examination or questions of the Judges as well, but we'll see. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you for handing the floor to the Defence. We would like to thank the witness and to say hello to everybody, but thank the witness to be so kind to come back. Thank you very much, Mr. Harding, for coming back. As it was the case in the past, I will put my questions to you in the French language.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: If you remember, you testified on the 25th and on the 26th of February of this year. And since some time has lapsed between those dates, I would propose, Mr. President, that we begin by showing the witness a map that he himself had annotated so that he may refresh his memory this way. I will give the map number or the indication. I believe that it is marked P -- I cannot remember any more what was the mark. I believe that the court clerk has it in front of you. Yes, I found it. It's P3644. It is a Prosecution evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is H, actually. So 3644H.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So 3644H.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it PH?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm very sorry, it is a handwritten -- it is a handwritten letter. I believe it is an"H" now that I look at it better. May we show this map to Mr. Harding, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I have a map, P3644.CH.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] It should be that. It should be that, yes. While the witness is examining the map, I would like to ask the court clerk to prepare as well a map that the Defence had submitted to the witness last time. It is a map bearing the mark D53 or 54, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Great.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you please take a few moments to look at this map, or do you have it clearly in your memory? Do you need some time?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can remember this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. I would also like to submit to you the map bearing the number D53, only to refresh your memory, and then I shall put questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Usher, would you please be kind enough to show this map to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D53 be put on the ELMO. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If the Defence could please indicate the date of this map - it looks like a sketch to me - and also who the author is of this map. Because I suspect that this is a map which is attached to one of the witness statements from a Prosecution witness, and this Prosecution witness was in Sarajevo in 1993. So I'm not sure whether it's very helpful for this witness to comment to a map drawn by a witness who was in -- potential witness who was in Sarajevo much later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do remember that we paid some attention to shifting certain positions. But Mr. Piletta-Zanin, could you please explain what the source of this map is?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Mr. President. Would you like me to explain to you the meaning of this map, or the origin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Concerning the origin, unfortunately, I cannot do it. I thank you for asking me to do it, but unfortunately I cannot. I did not think that this objection would be raised at this point, so I am not prepared to give you this answer. But the Defence will look into it later on. I shall be able to give you an answer shortly after the break. But what my colleague is telling me is that these elements come to us from the Prosecution, and this is why it shouldn't be a problem. Now, as to know exactly who was the material author of this map, I do not know it. But I believe that concerning this document, it must bear an ERN number. I do believe that there is -- the authenticity of this document is not in question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... confusion as far as time is concerned whether it could confuse the witness when he would be confronted with a map which is covering a different period of time compared to the period of time he is testifying about. I think that was your problem, Mr. Waespi. What the source -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And the witness, who will be a Prosecution witness, is Witness Gardemeister-Kukkola, who will come later, and as I said before, he was in Sarajevo in 1993, well after Mr. Harding was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, of course, it is a document which originates from the Prosecution, so it can be used. But Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you're warned that this sketch or this drawing, as Mr. Waespi says, stems from a different period of time. So if you would please keep that in mind. I don't know what questions you would have about this map. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Mr. President. The question related to this map were with regards to the chronology of various observation posts, whether we are talking about Papa posts or Lima posts. This is why this document is here, because we just wanted to establish the chronology of the existence of these observation posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: We shall not look or consult these documents for now, Mr. Witness. They may remain in front of you. But my first questions are basically general questions. Mr. Witness, would you be kind enough to remind us if that is correct that you stayed on the site from the month of July 1993 [sic] up until the beginning of the year 1993? Is that the correct period of time during which you stayed in Sarajevo, from July 1992 until 1993, the end of the year? Could you please tell us when were you there?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Sarajevo or in theatre?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When I talk about the theatre, theatre, I'm talking about Sarajevo, in the sense that during -- when were you in Sarajevo and if you intend to talk about Lima, that's also the case, you may do so.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only talk about the Papa side, and I was in Sarajevo August 1992 through to January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. I had thought that you said July. I'm terribly sorry. You yourself have now mentioned August 1992. I will take that into account. Do you know if there was an agreement, a cease-fire agreement, prepared on the 19th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that period, there was a cease-fire agreement about every other day. So it would be quite normal to have one, and it would be broken by 1000 hours on the day that it applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, who was implementing these cease-fires on the Serbian side, for instance?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could only comment on the Papa side. The Serbian side is the Lima side. I would be informed of a cease-fire by the operations staff in the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you know who would sign these cease-fire agreements?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say, it was somebody on the headquarters staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you talk about the headquarters staff, are you talking about the Serbian headquarters side?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm referring to my headquarters, being in the PTT building. In that building, there were liaison officers from both sides, and there were numerous senior officers that liaise with the French battalion based at the airport. And through that link and through those methods of communications, a cease-fire would be agreed. And that's the way that I understood it. But I was never part of a wide-area cease-fires, only very local cease-fires to achieve specific tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, you just told us that there was some liaison officers from each of the factions that were present, for both factions. Is that what you're telling me?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: From both sides, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. You told me that these officers were in direct liaison with the headquarters, therefore, the headquarters of both of the two sides, two factions, that were present?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer, Mr. Witness. I can therefore infer from the answer you just gave us that the headquarters, having been at the time under the responsibility of General Galic, because he was in charge of Sarajevo, so he would send his liaison officer every second day, every other day, in order to get a signature for a cease-fire, to come to a cease-fire agreement?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether he sent somebody to be physically present in the PTT or it was done through lines of communication, I can't answer that as I was never part of a general cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. However, the headquarters that were under the responsibility of General Galic, those headquarters made sure that somebody or somehow the message for a cease-fire would be sent to you or somebody would physically come and make sure that the cease-fire is implemented. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say, I was never part of the negotiations for arranging a general theatre cease-fire, area cease-fire, only local. So what actually physically happened in the PTT, I was never present as I was always out on an observation post or down in the city at the Papa headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for the answer. Thank you for this answer, Witness. Do you know if there was an operation done by the BiH army from Sarajevo that would be called Jug, J-u-g?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never heard of a specific operation as I was not there to comment on their tactical operations, really. I never heard of that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer, Witness. I would now like to go back to those two observation posts. I would like to talk about the Papa observation post. I believe that phonetically the abbreviation stands for "Presidents." You told us that there were five Papa posts, and then later on a sixth Papa observation post was implemented. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number designations are correct but it does not mean that there were six specific posts manned by UNMOs. To avoid any confusion, when a new position was put in place, it was the next number on, whereas we would remove people from an observation post but that position still maintained a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, while you were still working at the Papa posts, I believe 1 and 5, you knew nevertheless that outside there were some observation posts called Lima. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you know what is the reason why there has never been, as it seems, observation posts, Lima observation posts, at the southeast of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't comment on where any of the Lima posts were because I was never informed of where they were because I did not need to know. Likewise, my opposite number on the Lima side, he didn't know exactly where the Papa side observation posts were. So whether there was one in that position or not, I wouldn't know. And whether he tried to put one in there, again, I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, were there any Papa zones to the southeast of Sarajevo? Were there observation posts called "Papa" to the southeast of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can you tell us which one, please.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Papa 6, which I'm pointing to on the map. It was directly south of the Bistrik barracks on, I think the hill is referred to as Colina Kapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you know if there was an observation post independently of its name, whether it's Papa or Lima, but an observation post that was supposed to observe the Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only observations that we would do on Mount Igman would have been from Papa 5, which is in the west end of the city, and that looked directly west over the plain, and then you could see on the right-hand side down to Dogude [phoen], across the plain, up to Mount Igman. Whilst I was there, we tried to negotiate a position, a Papa position, on Mount Igman, but we were unsuccessful, whilst I was there anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, when you say that you were unsuccessful, what do you mean by that? Somebody stopped you from erecting an observation post?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Mount Igman once with a colonel and where we wanted to put it, I don't think they wanted us to be there for some reason. And there was also questions of accessibility to where we needed to go, and then as we are moving in trees, the routes would have to be clearly identified because it would be easy to confuse our movements with movements from the ABiH. There was only one trip up there whilst I was there. It was then held with the colonel to continue negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, thank you. Just to make sure who was the authority, which camp was the side with which you were trying to negotiate?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be the ABiH forces on Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, thank you for your answer. I should now like to discuss military operations. Are you aware of a military operation whose name was Kisik, K-i-s-i-k?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Yeah, I was bothered by an interpretation I received, but it's fine now. I have another series of questions for you regarding your knowledge of weapons and what was happening in your area of responsibility; that is, the Papa posts generally speaking. You mentioned the existence of 50 guns at Papa 1, and these were guns, I think, that you defined as 120-millimetre guns. Is my memory correct?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you clarify what you actually said regarding the number first.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the exact transcript of what I said. I believe there were only four 105-millimetre artillery pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Exactly, yes. 105-millimetre, I'm sorry, I apologise. Yes, 105 millimetre, not 120. And there were 50, is that right, at Papa 1? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: How many then?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four. Four. It's only four.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Could you indicate, Witness, what is a 105-millimetre weapon?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by indicate? Do you want a picture or a small comparison --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, Witness. But the person addressing you is no specialist in military weaponry, and I don't know what a 105-millimetre gun is. I don't know whether others are like me, with very limited knowledge, so I wondered if you could explain for us what a 105-millimetre weapon is.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, okay. I understand now. 105-millimetre artillery piece is fairly small, has two wheels, towed by a truck. It has quite a small barrel. Either side of the barrel and in front of the wheels are protection plates. The crew go behind these plates. The weapon has a sight. They are given the range and indication to the target, and then they would fire the weapon, which has a projectile which is 105 millimetres in diameter and would have a range between 11 to 14 kilometres, depending on the model of the artillery piece and also the standard and condition of the ammunition and the skill of the crew and their communication as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, an artillery piece of 105 millimetres, is that in fact an artillery piece or not?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. You stated in your previous statement that there were crew members for this piece who had no previous training in military warfare. Can you confirm that? Is that what you told us?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You also said, Witness, that the majority of these men were men who had no protection helmets or uniforms. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I proceed from the principle that these people were dressed in civilian clothes. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had a collection of pieces of uniforms. Some were in uniform. The temperature at that time would mean that they would be in shirt-sleeve order or T-shirts. And if they got camouflage trousers, you could construe that to be a complete uniform. Other ones didn't have any specific items of military uniform. It would just be jeans. So there was a mix.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, those who didn't have any camouflage clothing or helmets or anything at all and who were wearing jeans, would you agree with me in saying that they were dressed in a civilian manner?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be civilian clothing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, at the beginning of the war, and I mean more precisely the time when you arrived, that is, the summer of 1992, the month of August 1992, is it not right to say that many soldiers did not have uniforms in the sense that one means in a regular army?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in that there was not enough equipment to go around.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, is it also true that there wasn't enough offensive equipment? What I mean is one gun for four men or one gun for five men.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, there was not enough small arms to go around.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you know if one of the strategies of the ABiH was that the weapons would remain in situ, that is, on the front line, on the positions, whereas the men would take turns manning those weapons? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whilst I was there, there was no ammunition for these artillery pieces and nobody manned them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I' talking about what you referred to as SA, that is, "small arms."

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they would hand over the small arms, the rifle, when one of them was on guard or something. They would have to hand it over as there was not enough to go around. So that was my confusion. [Realtime transcript read in error "there was more confusion"]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Witness. Do you also know whether the army, early on, organised some kind of platoons grouping around one weapon, four or five soldiers with one weapon, and there would be one weapon for those four or five soldiers? Does that ring a bell for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, just before the witness answers that question, I note a transcript error which may not get picked up in the check. That's page 14, line 4. Presently it reads, "there was more confusion." I think the witness said "that was my confusion."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that was my recollection as well but I was not following the English transcript. By saying this, Mr. Ierace, I'm certain that it will be corrected this evening. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you understand my question, Witness, please?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You've said "yes" twice. Is that an answer to my question?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand your question. Around the artillery pieces, they called themselves a battery and they named it the 105th battery. Around the small arms, which I think you are referring to, I saw that there were no divisions such as platoons or sections. The whole thing was just as a battery. So one weapon didn't belong to five; it would just go according to the rota for sentry duty and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Witness. Let us imagine, Witness, that one of those soldiers dressed in civilian clothing is wounded, mortally wounded. If you were to see him, what would -- on what grounds would you be able to say that this was a civilian or a military man who had been wounded? Have you understood my question?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand it. And for such an incident, if that were to occur, the report I would produce would be that my position had received incoming fire, and there was one casualty. If I were to take the casualty to the morgue or to the hospital, I would just refer to it as a casualty. So we didn't really have a delineation between somebody wearing military clothes or somebody wearing civilian clothes. And this is hypothetical because I was never put in that position to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But we do agree that hypothetically, if you were to find a wounded man along the front line or in the trenches dressed in civilian clothing, you could not exclude categorically that this was a military man, that this was a soldier?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way that we would describe that is that they were parts of a militia force, so as part of a militia, they do not have sufficient equipment. So physically I could describe them as wearing civilian clothes but it was that he was male, female, dead or alive, rather than reference to what he was wearing. So it will be difficult to give a finite answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Talking about militia, could you tell us, until when, as far as you know, did this militia remain active, knowing that you stayed until January 1993 in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: By a militia, it would be a specific group of people that are working to a common objective. And the front lines were manned for the entire time that I was in Sarajevo, and the people manning those had varying degrees of equipment. So I don't quite understand what you're trying to ask me. But all the front lines were manned when I left. Some were manned by uniformed people and some not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Let me rephrase my question. You yourself spoke about militia a moment ago. Were you referring to what was known as the "Territorial Defence"?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: By a "militia," that would indicate it was not a paramilitary organisation, as a militia is quite a specific group of people. I haven't come across the term "Territorial Defence" before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you define briefly and succinctly what you mean by militia?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Militia would be a group of people drawn into a conflict, working to a common aim, commanded by a common headquarters and undertaking military training as and when the conflict would allow and would do effectively what's commonly known as on-the-job training. Before the conflict, they would not be in the military and so would have minimum knowledge of military operations. Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. You have certainly answered a part of the question, Witness. Witness, so these militia were not wearing uniforms because they were basically clothed in civilian clothing?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because there was not enough military uniforms to go around.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. But if these militia were active on the front, they were armed, some better, some worse. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Witness. Witness, could one say that these were, in a sense, civilians who armed themselves for a purpose X, defence of barricades or anything else? Would that be right?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Working to a common aim, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: As you have repeated what I said, so armed civilians pursuing a common aim. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I think I heard you correctly. I don't know whether the transcript will reflect it. Could you repeat your answer? It has not been reflected in the transcript. You said "correct," did you not?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. They were armed civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me now go on to another group of questions concerning heavy weapons in Sarajevo, and not armed militias that we have just been discussing but heavy weaponry. Witness, could you please look again at this map to your right, the topographic map and not the sketch. You spoke to us during your last hearing. You spoke to us about shelling that occurred from a position close to post 6, I think it was, with a weapon which was moving laterally, I think you said. Do you recollect this fact?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, traversing, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you, to refresh our memories, tell us briefly where this took place? Where did the firing come from?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the area that's marked on this map, where I'm pointing now by the blue arrow that points to the north with a short line through the centre of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, Witness. You have told us that the shells fired from this position landed on the town. Could you please remind us where they landed?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Firing from the position I've just said, over my head, and I was at position 6, on the map in blue, and the landing on the roof tops in the centre of the city and then traversed to the right and to the left in this area marked with the letter "I."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, in answer to a question from the Prosecution, you said that in your opinion, this was shelling of a civilian area. Do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was a civilian area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, last time I put to you a certain number of questions to see whether you could localise with precision the address of the headquarters of the 1st Corps and the address of the brigades, and you told us that you could not. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, do you know where the MUP was, M-U-P, the MUP?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never heard that term before.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, if I were to tell you that within the 1st army corps, the MUP had its headquarters in the area that you yourself marked, would you believe that this was still a shelling of civilian area when there were important military targets there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think since the witness said he doesn't know what MUP is, I'm not sure whether it's very helpful if he is asked whether the headquarters of such an unknown quantity for the witness was a military target or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that if the witness doesn't know what the MUP is, which has been described as the police academy or secret service, he certainly knows what the 1st army corps is, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said the MUP was in the 1st army corps. That's what the translation --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll just read the English transcript. Witness, if I were to tell you that within the 1st army corps, the MUP had its headquarters in the area that you yourself marked, that's what the translation says.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but I was focussing on the question that within that area was both the MUP and the 1st corps, and the headquarters of the 1st army corps, which are two different targets, one next to the other. The MUP is in Benevolencija Street, and the 1st Corps right next to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we can't check exactly what you said in French, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, but still the objection says that if you don't know what the MUP is, then you should take that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can rephrase it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, if I were to tell you, and that is what I think I told you a moment ago, that within this area there were two targets, one, the headquarters of the 1st army corps, and secondly, the services of what is known as MUP, which -- police institution of great importance, as a specialist, would you then consider that to be a military target?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer would be that the firing of that weapon is completely indiscriminate. If the location of the headquarters were known, then you would use a specific weapon to fire at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, my question does not concern the weapon. It only relates to the presence of military targets, a headquarters of the 1st army corps. Is that something that is also sometimes defined as police academy or are these military objectives, objectives of a military nature?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps headquarters would be a military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. When you say all headquarters, Witness, do you mean the headquarters of a brigade for instance as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just a clarification. Maybe my friend hasn't read the transcript. I think he answered, "The corps headquarters would be a military target" and not "all headquarters."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is what is in my recollection as well. So of course, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, might not follow the English transcript but it should be corrected if it's not correctly in there. May I remind you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that when the witness asked you -- answered your question about the military target, that your question was about shelling. You said, "I'm not talking about the kind of weaponry," but you were talking about shelling when you initially asked your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I don't see where the problem is, Mr. President. I said that I was leaving light weapons to go on to heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When the witness answered that it would have been an indiscriminate -- what does he exactly say? It was an indiscriminate -- you said, "I'm not talking about weapons" but your question was about shelling, so about heavy weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. But at first, what I wanted was simply to be told whether we are talking about a military target or not. The question of whether this or that weapon was being used comes next. This was -- I was talking about the location in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Well, of course, shelling is not a weapon, but we use that word for heavy arms. So you are using that word in your question, so if you say, "I was not asking about that," you did ask about shelling in that area. You asked whether the shelling was on a civilian target or not. But let's leave it for the moment. But please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'm continuing, Witness. You said that the headquarters of an army corps would be a military target. Witness, would the headquarters of a brigade also be a military target?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that NATO brigade or some other formation? A NATO brigade is thousands of men. I'm not sure how you break up brigades.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question, first of all, because I'm not a military expert and secondly because, at the time, I don't know whether the BH was a member of NATO. I think not. And therefore, I'm talking about a brigade in the general sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: How large is your brigade?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: It's not my brigade, but a brigade generally has 2 and a half thousand to 3.000 men, I think.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then a brigade headquarters is a legitimate military target.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Witness, in view of the involvement in the conflict of police forces, would the headquarters of the police of the same level of command also be military targets?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The question presumes two things: Firstly, an awareness on the part of the witness, with some precision, as to whether the police at all times were combatants. There is not that evidentiary basis for the question to be asked. And secondly, it's a matter for the Tribunal to finally determine. The question is inappropriately asked of this witness unless there is some particular expertise that the Defence draws upon of this witness. At this stage, that hasn't been established. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. The question that I asked was what is sometimes known as a mirror question, that exactly the opposite is asked to what the Prosecution asked: Wasn't this indiscriminate shelling of a civilian area? What I'm doing now is to try and establish a balance. And if we had command centres of the police of that level, would that not be a military target? And I'm only doing what the Prosecution has done but the mirror opposite. And I think that the Defence cannot be prevented from asking such a question because, on the one hand, the witness is a man, with his military expertise, can clarify things for all of us. And secondly, if the witness cannot answer, he has only to tell us that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, a military man such as this witness can certainly comment on whether military headquarters are a legitimate military target. That is uncontroversial. We have heard evidence in this trial to date that reserve police officers undertook a military role. We have also heard evidence that regular police officers didn't. There has been some qualification of that as well. There is not an evidentiary base that this witness speaks of which allows the Defence to go the next step and invite the witness to declare whether a police headquarters in the context of Sarajevo in the context of August 1992 to January 1993 was a legitimate military target. That is the difference between a police station and military headquarters in relation to this witness's opinion. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harding, may I ask you a question in between. Do you have any knowledge of involvement of either regular police or reserve police in the combats, in the military activities in the period when you were there, of course?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw a policeman on the front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but my question is whether you have any knowledge of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- involvement of the police, either reserve or regular, in the military activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the police were just the civilian side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I think it's not of great use to ask hypothetical questions on the issue to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you, Mr. President. I shall, therefore, ask another series of questions of a different nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: With regards to heavy weaponry, Witness, you have told us that your services were to observe, to check and surveil the mobile means enabling the firing of mortar shells by making them mobile; in other words, by moving them from point A to point B. Which were those mobile means? Would you please be able to describe to us what they were?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may have been confusion, as we didn't monitor any mobile mortar units whilst I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, did you not state that there were mobile means and that you were also in charge of tracing them and discovering them, in other words?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whilst I don't have my transcript, if mortars had been reported firing from an area, I may well have been tasked to go to that area, such as a hospital. But invariably, we would be chasing things that would have moved on, if they were there in the first place. So we didn't monitor mobile mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, when you talked about firing from the Kosevo Hospital, you stated that you did not personally see any traces on the ground coming from the use of mortars. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You stated, and I'm talking about your statement on page 4375, that apparently those mortars would have been mounted on something. Would you please tell us, according to you, what were these mortars mounted on?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not having a copy of that transcript in front of me, I would say it would have to have been something mobile. I may well have said a truck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please indicate the line for me, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. I have page 4375 --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, Mr. President, I worked on the French transcript, I must say. So I do not know if the pages are the same. But of the French transcript, it is on page 4375 and the lines in question are the lines 11 and 12. This is only the French text, however. I could probably be able to find you the English text, but what I have in the French version is that it was probably mounted on something else. And in fact, later on, if you wish, I could give you some time to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I have some difficulties in finding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you like me to search for it in the English transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... already.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps if we can assist Your Honours, it's on page 4373, on line 16, and it -- well, perhaps if my friend wants to use it, he can put it to the witness himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask the witness to move closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I still have difficulties. Did I understand you well you said 4373, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then line?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: 16. It starts on line 15, "But I didn't see any base plate marks." And then it continues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I must have a different transcript then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. The one I am using is the uncorrected Microsoft version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said "plates." I could look for "plates" and that would certainly give me --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: "Plate marks."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just found the English transcript. I opened it, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've found it with the search engine. It's 4364, line 7, in the final version. Let me tell you, Mr. Harding, what the question was at that moment on the 25th of February and what your answer was. The question was: "You said that you checked the area around the Kosevo Hospital and tried to find the location of the mortar. And you mentioned these markings, the plate marks. So did you observe or did you observe any such marks?" Your answer was: "I found no marks on the ground to suggest that a mortar had been firing." I still have no mobility yet. The next question was: "So if a mortar was fired, apparently the evidence is if that mortar was fired, what kind of mortar use would that have been?" And your answer was: "The staff sergeant didn't specify a calibre, but it was going to be noticed." I still do not get at the mobility of --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Continue reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the mobility will come actually at a later point. I just wanted to establish this for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last part of this answer was, "But I didn't see any base plate marks, and therefore it must have been mounted on something different." That was your answer. Now, please, repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, let's go to the next page of the transcript actually. If it was mounted on something, this something, could it have been mobile? Could it have been a truck, for instance, technically speaking, of course?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you have stated on the following page that the forces, the UN forces for which you were working, asked you to verify if those trucks, such trucks actually were moving throughout the city and if they were actually used. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If he indicates, my learned friend, a specific answer by the witness, it will be helpful for the witness, especially after that happened a month ago that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely, with pleasure. However, I just wanted the witness to say it for himself. I'm not going to give him his answer. I may read you his answer. The answer was: "Yes, you were asked to look for such means, but you and your men had not found any."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you confirm this, Witness? I'm talking about mobile means, of course.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were tasked to look for things and we never found any. But we would have reported such --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, thank you for this answer. Witness, is it possible to carry in a civilian vehicle, a simple ordinary civilian vehicle such as for instance a Golf VW, not to mention the precise vehicle, a small mortar calibre, 80 millimetres, for instance? Witness, could you please say your answer out loud.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: A small car, you could carry it. Whether you could fire it, I wouldn't be able to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But it is absolutely possible to mount and to transport such a device, to actually fire from a vehicle and then to dismantle it and to leave with the same vehicle. Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, my friend packs into his question now several issues, and I think the witness already said that he could not comment on whether it could be fired with it. And that's one of the aspects he has asked again. So if my learned friend could just divide his questions into subquestions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it is not quite the same question. The witness said, "To fire from a vehicle, I don't know." And consequently, I was already subdividing my question. But my following question was: "Is it possible to carry it, to mount it outside, to fire, to dismantle it, and then to bring it back in the same vehicle such mechanism? Is it possible? Is such a mechanism possible?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those three stages, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer, Witness. Such a mobile device that hypothetically would be moving around the city, is it a legitimate military target when one uses the firing called a "counterbattery firing"?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: A counterbattery firing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would have more questions, but I don't know at which time you wish to take your break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, we started at a quarter past 2.00, so we'll have a break at a quarter to 4.00. Another 15 minutes. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Then I shall continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, thank you for giving us such precise answers. Witness, did you see in Sarajevo during your stay there civilian Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. vehicles that would have stickers either on the dash or on the windows of the vehicle?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stickers, what do you mean by "stickers"? Because yes, they have stickers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: By "stickers," I mean stickers that would identify a vehicle as being a military vehicle.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw many vehicles. And if they were military ones, they tended to be painted green and painted by hand. But there were a lot of vehicles being moved around, a lot of white Volkswagen Golfs, for example. But specific stickers, I can't recall such things because it has been nearly ten years ago now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you were talking to me about a white Golf or white Golfs. Were those vehicles requisitioned by the army?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told but I never confirmed that they came from the Volkswagen factory which was to the north of the city. I think it's in the area of Vogosca. I saw -- I had a chance to look at it once through a pair of binoculars, and I saw a lot of white Volkswagen Golfs still parked there. There were an awful lot of them. Whether they had been requisitioned or acquired, I was never able to confirm that, if that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: All the answers satisfy the person that asks questions. But with regards to this vehicle, Witness, did you know if the drivers were able to find fuel easily?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I can't answer that question really because --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So then during your mission there, when we talk about pumps, gas stations, were they distributing gas on a regular basis to civilians? Were they operating normally?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that question. That would be UNHCR. I got my fuel from the PTT and French battalion. So I don't know if they had difficulty finding their own. I really can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for this, Witness. I would like to go back to the hospital now and still with relation to heavy weaponry. We had a witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Mr. President, I believe that we can talk about a previous testimony heard without referring to the witness in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But we have heard a witness testifying to the effect that the hospital had undergone direct firing from the inside of the city. Were you able, as an observer, to examine traces of these -- of the shootings on the Kosevo Hospital which would have been direct shots coming from inside the city and not from outside the city?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The damage that I inspected was on vertical sides of the hospital and so did not come from the city centre. They were north-facing slopes -- north-facing walls, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, still with regards to the hospital, is it technically possible that one may have opened the fire with mortars, either small-calibre mortars or large-calibre mortars, from the roof of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The roof, technically, I suppose, it would be possible to fire from a roof, but I didn't look at the roof. Looking at it from that position, it didn't really occur to me from the roof, because that's not where the staff sergeant indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you know if a team of observers checked the roof of the hospital to see if some mortar traces were found there?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we wouldn't go up there at that time. And none of my troops went up there to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. I would like us now to move on to the PTT building. We are talking about the central building of the PTT that you have in memory. Is that correct? Is that so? Thank you. Now, could you please turn to the map that's on your right and tell us, where is the central PTT building, please? Witness, would you kindly show us on the map that area.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The PTT --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You are talking about point P. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, just to avoid any confusion, would you be able to show us where was the Presidency, and I would like to check on this map. The Defence was not in possession of one. I just wanted to know if the president was not written as well, indicated as well with a letter P. Would you please be able to tell us where the Presidency was as well?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you mention this with regards to the map?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, let's move on to --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, my friend, the witness, I think, wanted to answer or at least explain where he pointed -- he has pointed to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what you intended to do, Mr. Harding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, because the HQ is adjacent to the Presidency. So that is not the exact position of the Presidency. If the Presidency is regarded as the main building in the centre of the city, we were immediately east of it in an adjacent building, and that's Papa headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that my learned friend, Mr. Waespi, is giving me his wonderful support. I shall certainly hope that this cooperation will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But Witness, would you please go back to the map. Turn it around, flip it around, please, and put it back where the PTT building is. I believe it's on the other side of the map. Thank you. That is correct. We can see on our screen point "P," which represents the PTT building, and right under -- over it, actually, we can see point 5. I believe that that represents the Papa 5 post where you were at some point. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's Papa 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Very well. Witness, how were you able to communicate when incidents would occur between the Papa positions and the Lima positions?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Papa side never communicated with Lima side. It was always with the PTT, and we were on different radio frequencies.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, in order to communicate between the two, between you and the others, you were using the PTT structures. Is that correct, PTT devices?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The UN-supplied radios, if that's what you mean, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I have no doubt that you were using UN devices. But were you actually using, in the proper sense of the word, the technical assistance in terms of networking? Were you using the local PTT for its network?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I first arrived, the telephones still worked, but we would still use the radio. Administration would be carried out using the telephone. After a while, the power went down, and so we only had the radios.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, if at the very beginning you were using the PTT installations, do you know if the government, the said government army was also using PTT installations for their own needs?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the telephone worked, then I would expect them to use it. Yeah, it's reasonable.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, did I understand you directly, did you say, in fact, that the civilian PTT were also being used for military communications? In terms of means, when we talk about civilian installations, were the military using those installations? At least at the very, very beginning.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I first arrived, I had very little contact with the ABiH. But if the telephones worked, then I would presume that they would use them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: In other words, the civilian PTT infrastructure was actually being used for military communications? Were they assisting the military?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, if the telephone worked, then I would expect them to use it. But once they went down, then it was just radios. So I can't really comment from experience, only from a personal judgment type of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Witness, do you know if at the beginning in fact the army, so-called government army, had for themselves very important radio communications which were enabling them to be in touch with the other army corps throughout the whole Bosnia, and this, of course, was in the general concept of the defence?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess they had their own communications setup, so how they went about that, I didn't have any experience of it. But I'm sure that they had their own communications, if that answers the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, when you say "I suppose," do you know for sure or do you just infer this?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can't run an army without communications. Therefore, I would presume that they had communications and an army in a modern-day context, rather than historic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So are you telling me that communications means are indispensable for an army?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a significant advantage to have communications, if that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have a few short questions, but I do believe it would be quite important to take a break right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... until quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you may proceed in cross-examining the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, the name of Major Henneberry, does it say anything to you? Does it ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Henneberry, Canadian army?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Maybe indeed, Major Henneberry. Is his rank major?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Was this commander active during the time that you were in Sarajevo? Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Major Henneberry was another military observer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you work with him, Witness?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm trying to remember. He may well have been on the headquarters staff. He wasn't one of my staff on Papa side. So whilst I recognise the name and connect to the service, I can't recollect any actual dealings with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, but did you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only on a professional basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should now like to read a statement, two and a half lines or three lines in English, of a statement made by this Major, Mr. Henneberry. May I do so? And after that, I will have a question for the witness. This is Exhibit 0106-2851.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What's the nature of this document? Is it a witness statement or is it an attachment to a witness statement or a document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have an extra copy so in order to give Mr. Waespi the opportunity to have a look at it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have a copy, Mr. President. But it is simply a statement of a witness taken by representatives of the Prosecution and which we have in front of us. But there are only three lines that I would like to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think usually, there's no objection, Mr. Waespi, or? Usually --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We would like to see the statement before it's quoted to the witness or even shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, usually, if you are quoting from a certain document, the other party is informed about at least the use of the document. So if you could just give it for Mr. Waespi perhaps for one minute so that he can have a look at it. I can expect the Prosecution to be prepared for prior statements of this witness but, of course, not of every witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which line do you intend to quote, Mr. Piletta-Zanin? You have given it away now, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Is it the bit you have indicated, my friend, with blue ink?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think it is the one but last paragraph on this page, three lines. But the document was produced by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: We have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to read to you what was stated by the military officer that we were referring to a moment ago, this major in the Canadian army, regarding the 3rd of December, 1992. [In English] "... news said Serbs shelled airport. We watched and reported Muslims shell airport from Mount Igman, Ilidza. (Again, the news reports were wrong and the wrong side took the blame internationally for actions they didn't start.)" "The wrong side took the blame for actions they didn't start." [Interpretation] Thank you. Witness, were you informed of shelling that took place on the 3rd of December, 1992, of the airport shelling from Mount Igman?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only shelling that I recorded and can note on the 3rd of December was the offensive on Otes, and we had no observation posts on Mount Igman and we had nobody off to the west side of the plateau over towards Ilidza or Butmir, so I wouldn't be able to comment on anything coming out of Mount Igman or behind Mount Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Witness. Mr. Richard Mole, was he your superior?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a period of time when I was in Sarajevo, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you remind us of that period of time?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Mole left Sarajevo on the 24th of December, 1992, and Lieutenant Colonel Cutler took his place. As to when he moved in, I cannot give you an exact date of that, but it would have been approximately September 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know, Witness, whether Mr. Richard Mole made a statement, like you, for this Tribunal, a written statement?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand he has been approached, but whether he made a written statement, I don't know. I have spoken to him purely out of courtesy but not with specific regard to any activities or any specific incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you, Witness. Let us assume that commander Richard Mole did make a written statement, and let us also assume that he said, and I will summarise the following, that the Sarajevo forces, that is the so-called governmental forces, placed certain weapons in the vicinity of the Kosevo Hospital. Unfortunately, I only have the text in Serbian, which says, "in the vicinity of the Kosevo Hospital." Do you know whether we are talking here about other weapons than the mortars that it has been established were used in the vicinity of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. The witness my learned friend is referring to, that's Mr. Mole, will be a witness here. And I don't think it's appropriate for this witness to comment on something the originator of this witness statement can do himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm not asking for any comments on the statements of Mr. Mole. I'm just asking whether this witness also knows of any other weapons in addition to the mortars that were referred to being localised in the vicinity of the Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... any reference is necessary to another witness, which -- but of course, you can ask him the question if he -- perhaps the answer would be different than a confrontation. Another statement would be most helpful, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I took the liberty of doing this. It is only because I wanted to know whether this witness worked in a team with Mr. Mole who saw this, so that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. You're not asking for any comments but asking for information known to the witness personally. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat my question, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you see in the vicinity of Kosevo Hospital other weapons or guns in addition to the mortars that we referred to a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were the armoured personnel carriers which we have spoken about before. But any other weapons like mortars or anything like that, then no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What do you mean, "armoured vehicles," Witness? You're referring exclusively to what is known as the APCs?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Armoured vehicle, APC, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Witness, are you aware of firing in the period while you were in Sarajevo that came from the position Papa 4 in the direction of the PTT?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. As for men, you said during your testimony that you knew that there were about 50 men at Papa 1, and 50 at Papa 4, approximately. Would you agree with those figures as being those that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Approximately, thank you. How many men were there at the other posts that may be of interest to us, that is number 2, 3, 5, and possibly also post 6, if you know? And when I say 5, I mean 5A and B.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Papa 6 is 0. Papa 5, 0. Papa 5A, 0. Papa 5B, 0. Papa 2, 5. I think that covers it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So these men you are referring to, you are referring to soldiers of what is called the "government army," are you not?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if -- that's military personnel, militia personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, if I add up -- if I add up, you're talking of the staff of the government army of Sarajevo, are you not?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Talking about the people at those grid references, those positions, as numbered, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, but those people whose number you have given, we are talking about soldiers of the army, the so-called government army. We do agree, don't we?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, if I add up the number of those soldiers, would we agree that there were about 50 men at Papa 1, 50 at Papa 4, and maybe a dozen on the outside on the other Papas, which means that we are talking of a number of the order of 150 men. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's 112.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Even better. Witness, do you know how many active soldiers there were in Sarajevo during the period while you were there on the side of the army of Sarajevo that was called the government army?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not gather such tactical information. No, I can't give a total.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, if I say to you that more or less everyone agrees that there were 75.000 soldiers recognised as such by the government army, would that figure be acceptable for you?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a general consensus, as I couldn't give a figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, if the observation groups at Papas 1 to 6 monitored or supervised some 120 soldiers, who took care of the others, that is, roughly speaking, some 84.000 that remained?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The observation post --

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The observation posts have interlocking arcs, which means from one, on its left, it would look towards another observation post. We were not there to supervise the troops, as they could do as they wanted, but we could observe 95 per cent of Sarajevo and its environs. When we saw military activity, we gave a grid reference which would be six figures, which brings it down to a 100 metre square. We did not allocate which side was doing at that grid reference. We simply reported the military activity as we were unarmed military observers. We were there not to count people or supervise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
