utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Witness. A few more technical questions with regard to the city. Do you know what Zetra is?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You never heard any mention made of the Olympic stadium to the north, close to the Kosevo Hospital? A hangar close to the Kosevo Hospital.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Olympic stadium, as in the running track and open area in the middle, was one of the Papa positions. We referred to it as the "Olympic stadium" rather than an area name such as if that's what Zetra is. But yes, I know about the Olympic stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know whether there were any hangars or halls that were used as hangars close to that area?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Olympic stadium that I talk about had seating all the way around, and underneath it was where we had some military observers. I walked around approximately half of that -- you could get vehicles parked in there, if that's what you mean by hangar. But in the middle of the stadium was grass, it was a football pitch. And when I first arrived you could not go out into that area because it was covered by a sniper. So by "hangar" I would infer an aircraft. No, you couldn't get that under the stadium seating.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, but next to the stadium, was there a covered area which was used as a hangar or as a warehouse and that was called Zetra?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: South of the stadium, there was a large structure that I was informed used to be the indoor ice skating rink, and that had severe impacts that I saw on the roof, and was burnt out. I had no cause to go into just a burnt-out building. We only went to the stadium as I've described.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you see equipment, military equipment, or troops next to that structure that you said was partially burnt?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I recall. There were people around, but I didn't really pay much attention. We just drove on past that road. It was going towards the front line there, and the building was burnt out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you know or do you not know whether there was any ammunition dump of the army there?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that would be the first I've heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, Witness. Do you know whether the schools were used during the conflict also for the stationing of troops?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you say "no," does that mean that you didn't know or that you are disputing it?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No -- no, I don't know where any of the schools were, either civilian or military.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know, Witness, whether there were special prisons in Sarajevo opened during the time, of course, that you were there?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that would be outside of my operations. In the PTT building were members of the Canadian Royal Mounted Police, and they would have dealt with that, I would presume, but not me as a military observer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, when you arrived in Sarajevo, that was in the summer of 1992, was it still possible to see active so-called paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing that I witnessed were the militia that we've spoken about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But you did not see paramilitaries on one side or the other?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: By "paramilitary" I presume that you mean a small group of people working to their own objectives, and no, I was out on an observation post and so had no experience of paramilitaries from either side, and I had no connection with Lima side for my entire period there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, when incidents occurred, so-called sniping incidents, what would happen in terms of information? To whom would you communicate that an incident had occurred, if to anyone?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the incident had been witnessed by an UNMO, he would then report it using the instant report, and that would go to Papa headquarters, and then into PTT. But only if he witnessed it. If he was told about it but didn't witness it, he could not report it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yourself, did you ever report such an incident of which you were a witness, an eyewitness, for instance?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was sniped at myself, but I didn't report it as it was just an incident I shouldn't have -- I should have paid more attention to where I was going. I myself, apart from that, I was ambushed twice, and I did report it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you talked to us about the Presidency a moment ago, and you indicated it on the map with the pointer. Who was, in Sarajevo, the Supreme Commander of the armies, at the time of the offence?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Presidency was a civilian government and they came -- they would come and go. So it's difficult to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I will stop you right here. My question is the following: Who was, in term of the structure of the organisation, the Supreme Commander of the armies?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Presidency, I would presume Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Witness, where were the premises where Alija Izetbegovic would go and his services would be stationed? Was it the Presidency building?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, since you just told us that the Supreme Commander of the armies was Mr. Izetbegovic, and that the Presidency represented his -- was it a military target since he was stationed in the Presidency building?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that's how he was viewed, then you could say that as the government, the leader of the government, he is ultimately as the army is one of his unit -- not units, one of his departments, but he was the civilian head of it rather than a military head. When he came and went, it was covered by international press. That was how we would find out due to being next door to him. But I would presume because he was a civilian leader, there was an agreement between Lukavica and the Presidency that they would not shell each other's headquarters. That was the understanding that I was under, with my headquarters right next door to the main Presidency building. I cannot -- that was purely by word of mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You're telling us that there was an agreement to exclude from all shelling commanding zones in question. Is that what you're telling us, Witness?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: To shell the Presidency building with the civilian leaders would hinder any progress with regard to negotiations. I was under the understanding that on that basis, the Presidency building right next door to me was not going to be a specific target; likewise, if Lukavica came under attack, it would also hinder those discussions. So it is difficult for me to say if Izetbegovic, from my point of view, was not a military leader. He did not wear a uniform. He did not carry arms, but the armed forces are usually under the command of the civilian leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, who was, of course -- it became a military leader when the war was declared. But let me move on to something else which you just said -- I'll withdraw what I just said. What you said, Witness, you were not aware of any specific agreements that would have been passed between the parties, agreements which would implement that some zones were to be excluded from shelling?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only building that I was aware of was the Presidency, and that was purely by word of mouth. PTT undertook discussions like that, and I was not there to make any political comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, one or two questions more. Do you know if on the Lima side, were there also positions surveilling or observing sniping incidents?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would expect a Lima position to report all that it witnessed. So if it witnessed a sniper firing or was subjected to sniper fire, then I would expect it to report it as we were under a common remit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Were you -- between Papa and Lima, were you in telephone communication? Were you able to communicate in any other way?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think the witness has answered that already, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not know if the witness had answered if for within the Papa area or between, the communications that existed between Papa and Lima. This is what I wanted him to clarify in his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, would you be able to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any direct communications with anybody on the Lima side. It was all through the PTT.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if any investigation was made following incidents reported by Lima to Sarajevo authorities, the so-called Sarajevo authorities, with regards to sniping incidents or shelling incidents?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I was unaware of his activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if an agreement, an anti-sniping agreement, was in some way made and then implemented by General Galic? Do you know this?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't heard of any anti-sniping agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I move to rise to my feet by that question on the basis of Rule 90. If my learned colleague has instructions that General Galic indeed was a party to such an agreement during the tenure of this witness, then it is incumbent upon him, it is required by the Rules that he put that to this witness or otherwise indicate it to the Tribunal if it is inconsistent with the evidence of this witness. In other words, this is perhaps an example of where Rule 90 is not being followed as the Defence is required to follow it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I understood what my learned colleague just said. But what I wish to say here -- what I wish to obtain from this is that the Prosecution states that General Galic would be responsible for a campaign that he either organised or allowed to be organised, that the elements of a campaign be orchestrated. So he allowed the existence of this campaign. According to the Prosecution. But I would like to know if this witness would know what he would know of the facts that could have happened even after his stay in Sarajevo but that is covered by the period covered in the indictment. If this witness heard that the General Galic wished that this agreement be implemented and if he participated to the drafting of this agreement, then he will tell us. If he has not heard of anything like this, he will tell us that he hasn't. But if each time the Defence asks a question in order to find or to get closer to the truth, if every time we get structured objections by the Prosecution, we will not therefore be able to approach and get closer to truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, may I first notice that I'm a bit surprised that I now get two counsel to object against questions. That's not what we allowed the Defence to do and I think that's not the way the Prosecution should do it. I think Mr. Piletta-Zanin explained the relevance of the issue raised and -- although I still owe the parties, and it will come soon, a further answer on what I would say was a submission of the Defence, not a specific request, nor was it an application for ruling. But I think still this week, I'll explain why the objections from the Defence do not stand where they think that Rule 90(H) could not be applied. But here we see, I would say, a clear situation where the witness is able to give evidence, at least, that's what the Defence seeks, whether the witness is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the Defence. If we look at Rule 90(H)(ii), we started: "In the cross-examination of a witness who is able to give evidence relevant to the case for the cross-examining party, counsel shall put to that witness the nature of the case of the party for whom that counsel appears which is in contradiction of the evidence given by the witness." That means that if the witness has given evidence which would contradict the case of the Defence, then of course in order to -- I would say to protect the witness rather than anyone else, to protect him against any confusion or any uncertainty as what he is confronted with, then you should put the case to the witness. But as far as I see now, we are in a situation where the Defence seeks whether the witness is able to give evidence relevant to its case, but we have not entered yet a situation where the testimony of the witness has contradicted the case of the Defence. So for this moment, I would deny the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, certainly given Rule 90, that is the only conclusion that one could draw, that the witness's evidence has not contradicted the Defence case. In relation to the ruling that will be handed down later this week, there was a decision of another Trial Chamber handed down last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If you're aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I've thoroughly studied that decision, yes. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, as I try to catch up what I -- where I was before, some will probably say it's not as difficult, but I am now slightly confused. Witness, I will ask you the question. I will reiterate my question: Did you at any point, given your competence and given your military career and your experience in Sarajevo, had you heard at any point that General Galic would have participated, would have taken part, in the preparation of an agreement which would be called an anti-sniping agreement?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That General Galic would have been in negotiation with Colonel Mole or Colonel Cutler, once something had been arranged, then he would have informed me so that that could be monitored. But at the time and up to the time when I left, I wasn't informed of such an agreement. But he wouldn't have told me because it wasn't in place, and therefore, it was still on his agenda as in my colonel, be it Mole or Cutler.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, a few more questions relating to military technique. Do you know what orders are, what we technically call directives, actually?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Orders, yes; directives, I take is another word for orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When we talk about directives, can we say in military terms that those are general orders given at the level of the general headquarters given or issued towards army corps?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: A directive -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Is that the adequate term?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, a directive given to the corps, and then that would then disseminate down through the ranks and become specific orders in order to react to the directives given.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you please tell us what was your military rank once again?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time in Sarajevo, squadron leader, which is a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I see, squadron leader. Mr. Commander, as a military man, would it be possible that upon examining these directives, someone who is a military man such as yourself, a man who practices the military art, to read exactly what the number of men in terms of troops are ordered for a certain period of time, for certain areas?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Directive would not give the specific detail exactly how many people are to do what specific task. It would be up to the commanders, be it colonel level or lieutenant colonel, to detail specific tasks in order to comply with a directive, a directive given to the corps level to apply to the corps rather than each individual man. So as the orders -- as the directive comes down, it would change to orders, which then would be to specific tasks. And all of those tasks collectively would comply with the directive, if you can understand the dissemination as it goes down through the rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. In other words, and if I understood you correctly, upon examining the directives and then the orders, and now we're talking about corps, army corps and battalions which would be respecting the directive, so then it would allow practitioners such as yourself to bring answers to some questions such as troop movements, the need to get involved in certain military means. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps if the Defence could indicate whether he wants the witness to talk about his experience from the British army or from the Bosnia Serb army or from the ABiH, whether he thinks he has seen any of these, I think this would clarify the purpose for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I think that Mr. Waespi understood very well. I'm not talking about the rules that are applied in the Swiss army; I'm talking about the general principle of how an army is organised; and namely, in this particular event, what happened in Sarajevo. I'm not talking about the organisation of British army or of any other army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your question to the witness is that whether Mr. Harding could, from this directives, or at least a man in a similar position, could, well, deduce from the directives as you indicated to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That brings you down to the situation in Sarajevo, Mr. Harding. BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think you did, as a matter of fact, as Mr. Waespi asked you to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you're very alert. You do not miss anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But Witness, would you be able to answer the question I just asked you earlier?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reaction to directives would all depend on the army. NATO forces allow initiative, and from directives, there are implied tasks. Regarding the forces in Sarajevo, how they would react to directives for either side, I couldn't comment. I could only comment from the NATO side, and that is that initiative is allowed to cover the implied tasks by the directives. So if that answers your question, as I've got slightly lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: This only answers partially my question. I shall maybe formulate my question differently. Let's suppose for a moment that we are in the NATO organisation, the way that army is organised. Let's say we are in an army that was organised by NATO, and at the time I believe that Yugoslavia was part of NATO. I'm not certain of this. I do believe that it was, but I'm not absolutely certain. In this army schematic, is the examination of the directive --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps I can help my friend. I'm not aware that Yugoslavia was part of NATO at that time. And if that's a basis for what follows in terms of questioning, I would suggest to rethink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the parties compromise on whether the former Yugoslavia ever was part of the NATO? May I deduce from the smiles on someone's faces that the parties do agree that the former Yugoslavia was never a member of NATO? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my will is such, I would so much like Yugoslavia to be part of this nation-wide grouping that I was taking my dream as reality. But I know that one day dreams can become reality, and I do thank my learned friend, Mr. Waespi, to have corrected me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, when we talk about NATO, the examination of directives and then orders at the level of brigade, would that enable to deduct troop movements, how much men should be brought in, what structure should be made, what would be the span of the battle, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm really sorry to insist on this point. Mr. Harding was an UNMO observing what happened in Sarajevo during a brief period, and unless the Defence shows that he has intrinsic knowledge about the NATO directives, of ABiH directives, which the witness denied, I'm not just not sure it's helpful to ask these questions to this witness. There will be higher-level witnesses going to channels which would be more able to, and certainly military experts to answer these questions. I do object to going further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I thank Mr. Waespi infinitely. He reminds me of a point that I wanted to mention to you earlier and I was just actually forgetting it. A long time ago, we have asked to be able to consult directives and the orders. We have asked a long time ago of this, and the Prosecution tells us, and I'm sorry for using the Serbian expression, mala sutra, which means "never." So it is very important for me to consult this. I would like to know, I wanted to know what had happened in order to prepare for this witness. But the access to these documents is refused to me. So we are now finally asking openly and overtly when can we have access to these documents. You do know that these documents exist, they are here in this building, and this is my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... is not on the witness stand at this moment. It is one of the things we finished with last Thursday, and you know, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that I expressed as my view that the Prosecution would on short notice come up with what they had found and what they were able to give you access to. And I felt, as a matter of fact, that part of that, and -- well, you demonstrated more or less that I was not wrong -- that you're more or less asking Mr. Harding whether the material you expect access to be given by the Prosecution is as vital for the Defence as you deem it is. I think Mr. Harding has practical experience in -- from his career, so I wouldn't say that the question on what you could deduce from certain directives could not be asked to the witness. But the importance for the Defence case, of course, is a different matter. But I think that's -- we'll deal with the issue between the parties at the end of this afternoon's session when perhaps we could get an indication of when now exactly the Prosecution comes up. And if you would do it on a very -- on the level of factual experience, you may proceed examining Mr. Harding.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will then continue under reserve, which is the following ruling, that once again the Defence would like to point out that we have our hands tied and our wings are clipped because we do not dispose of all the information that exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So this being said, Witness, let's say if I take a grenade in my hand and I throw the grenade from the roof top of a building 20 metres high, what would happen to the ground?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would receive damage. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Mr. Waespi, is there any need for the Prosecution to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, there is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Harding.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honour, when making references to the transcripts as referred to before, I will refer to the unredacted Microsoft version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whenever you find a very specific word in the parts, please indicate it to me because that's easier to search than the word "army" or "uniform."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I will also read out the relevant passages because it has been some time the witness testified, so I think it may be easier for him to refresh his memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And if you could indicate the day, whether it was the 25th or the 26th of February, that would be helpful for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Harding --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm terribly sorry to interrupt, but you are referring to the text, the French text or the English text, so that I am absolutely certain of what you're talking?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The English text.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Harding, you were asked --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I apologise. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Harding, you were asked on the 26th of February, 2002, that was on page 4434, and perhaps the key word is "no-man's land" or "front line." You were asked to mark certain positions. And in doing that you explained that, in some areas, it was quite a ground to be classed as "no man's land" as it gave cover to neither side --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I'm not quite certain that "no-man's land" and "front lines" mean the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. We'll find it. Even if it's not exactly the same, I think Mr. Waespi was helping me to refer to a specific word in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. text which might assist me in finding the place. Whether it's the same or not is a different matter. Thank you, Mr. Waespi, and please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. So I'm continuing to quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: "So it's not going to be exact because it was effectively natural buffer zones caused by the lie of the land. But this is the approximate location that if we were to go near it, we would have to liaise with one or both sides because we would be going into an area of possible conflict." Now - and that's my question - how would that liaison procedure work with respect to the Bosnian Serb army? With whom would you talk?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be all through the headquarters staff in the PTT building, and they would use liaison officers that were in the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, do you mean by your point you're making here that you had to make contacts, that this was the result in going safely into the area you wanted to go to, this buffer zone or no-man's land?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's your expectancy, that talking to the other side, both sides, that they would ensure that you could safely go to the area?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in fact, was that the case?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that system was used numerous times to repair city utilities, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harding. The second point I wanted to clarify with you is on page 4448, and that is again the 26th of February, 2002. And the code word, Your Honours, is "coloured armband." You talked about the following, and I quote you: "I hesitate to call them an army," and you will later clarify which army you talk about, "because I did watch troop movements going northeast. Some had uniforms, some did not, but they all wore the same coloured armband on their left arm." My first question is, which army are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And my second point is, do you recall the colour of these armbands?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that specific event, it was either blue or red, but I cannot say exactly which colour that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall whether during the time you stayed in Sarajevo, the colour changed, the blue or red colour, or it remained the same throughout?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I -- that specific reference was to a specific military activity, and they all had the same colour for that specific military activity. Otherwise, they didn't wear any armbands. It was just to identify them. I think you're referring to operation towards Zuc, and so presumably they had that amount of material in that colour for everybody, and if they had another operation, I can't say whether they would change it or reuse the material that they already had.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you do recall that in a different operation, they also had armbands?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, there was only one other major military advance that was reported to me, and they did have colour armbands. But again, I couldn't tell you exactly what colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harding. The next point is "cable car." And perhaps you can refer to your map, Prosecution Exhibit 3644. You told us still on the 26th of February, 2002, on page 4462, that you can see, and I quote you: "By the cable car from low ground to higher ground..." And you continue. Can you indicate, please, on the map where this cable car is located. And if you could use the blue pen this time. Is there any sign perhaps which would indicate the cable car?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the map as presented, there is a black line clearly shown on the map to a peak --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps you can indicate by a dotted line the line of the cable car.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dotted line in blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And at the one end, perhaps the one closer to Papa 6, can you mark it with perhaps a CC, indicating that this dotted line is the line of the cable car.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The next point is, in fact, the next page in the transcript which is, in my version, 4463. You mentioned when asked by the Defence an incident which you described as follows, and I quote: "And I observed them as they shelled the PTT building. We timed the flight of their ammunition and the number of rounds that were fired. And they coincided exactly with what the PTT building was reported to me." My first question is, do you recall any casualties occurring at this shelling?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no casualties as reported to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Who occupied the PTT building at that time?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: UN personnel, which would have been elements of the Ukrainian battalion, the French battalion, the French field hospital was in there, the headquarters of the UNMOs for Sarajevo. So it was all the UN personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, can you tell us the date of this incident, if you want and if you have it with you, referring to your diary?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will need to refer to my diary to get an exact date of that. It is going to be in December or January because that was when we had Papa 6. I know it was late in the day. I can't specifically remember it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harding, seeing that you have difficulties in finding, may I just remind you that in your answer at that time, you were thinking about November. That's part of the transcript. You said, "I would have to look through my diary to give you an exact date, but it would have been when Papa 6 was in position and operational." And you were looking at November. So you were looking at November. That's what you said, at least. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm just trying to remember exactly when Papa 6 went in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask which line you have, because we don't have the same lines with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... 4530. It would then be line 10 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, may I ask you how many questions you still have? How much time would it take? Because if we would have a quarter of an hour to go, even if it would be a bit shorter, it's very uncomfortable, I think, for Mr. Harding to sit here and try to find. Perhaps then we could use the break and then have the last question put to him whether he had found the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harding, I can imagine how it feels that you want to find something. You can't find it at this very moment. So perhaps, Mr. Waespi, if you would first proceed and then we'll see how to solve this problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm moving on to the shelling incident of the 31st of October. This is referred to - I'm still in the part of cross-examination - on page 4474. And in answering a question by the Defence, you said, and I quote: "No, I cannot say where the shells came as I did not see any of them firing. I was merely in the middle of when they landed." Now, the day before, in examination-in-chief, you testified on page 4381, that was the day before, and I quote: "Observation posts were reporting seeing the impacts in the city by the sheer amount of fire in the city, landing in the city. It could only have come from outside the city, that being the Bosnian Serb army." So my question is merely for clarification purposes. Despite the fact that you did not see yourself the sources of fire, was there still information at your disposition that allowed you to come to a conclusion as to the source of fire in terms of from which of the confrontation lines the fire originated?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because none of the Papa call signs reported seeing or hearing any firing from along the front lines that they were near. The sheer amount of fire landing on the city was reported by all the Papa call signs. And so from that, it had to be from the outside, because of the amount of ammunition that was coming in. There was so much it could not have been fired from along the front lines, and the Papa observation post not see it because there would be muzzle flashes, there would be smoke from artillery pieces and from mortars. So you would see it and you would hear it. But all they were observing were the impacts into the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when you say, and I quote you, what you just said: "It had to be from the outside," which side of the confrontation line are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving to a next issue, that is on page 4477, and it's about sniper fire. When asked today, like the reference I just made, you mentioned that you were sniped at. First, can I ask you when that was? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give a specific date, but I know exactly where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Which is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want to know whether I can link this to -- I'm going to 489, and I don't see page 4470 mentioned by the Prosecution. So could they give us a more precise indication because we have a different system.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I apologise to my learned friend. The page reference --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Apologise again. The page reference is 4477. And perhaps a word you could enter is "carriageway," because the witness said that, and I quote: "To the east of Papa headquarters, there were signs on the corners of the road so that when you cross that road, you knew that you had to move quickly as a sniper had been firing down that road. To the west enroute to the PTT, we used the main carriageway, and it was not uncommon to be fired at when you crossed the road at the junctions."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that's page 4542, line 7 and following.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And I just finish the paragraph: "And the fire would come from the south."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Harding, you wanted to tell us where the location of that incident was.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was sniped at personally near Papa 5 Bravo as marked on the map in blue ink, the small blue triangle. The shot was fired from further down the hill to the west where I'm indicating now --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If I just can interrupt you at this point. Can you please use your blue pen, indicate the exact location you were at and from which the fire came from, from which side.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at the position marked 5 Bravo, and the shot uphill from down at the bottom of the valley there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If I can just reflect what the witness drew, he drew a blue arrow directly towards the position 5B, and position 5B was the position he said he was sniped at, where his exact location was. Is there anywhere near the railways?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The railways are at the bottom of the valley, the railway. You can see the railway lines are marked here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: If you could just indicate one part of the railway lines and draw a small line and also the letter R.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The witness just drew a dotted line with the letter R, leading towards the arrow he drew a few seconds ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, when you said in your testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Solely in order to avoid confusion, I think I read on the map, which is not mine, another R on the map. I'm not quite sure, but I think next to the Presidency, I think I saw an R, a letter R.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there would be no confusion since this R would be close to 5 Bravo on the map. But Mr. Waespi, if I may guide you, this Chamber has seen maps before in their lives, and I have never seen such a clear indication of a railway and even a railway plus more so. Otherwise, the maps will be fully covered with repetitious characters. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I entirely agree with Your Honours, and I'm sorry for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But perhaps to avoid any confusion, add W to the R so we know it's the railways. Just a W after the R which you have just indicated.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You said that you did something foolish or silly which led to you being sniped at. Can you tell the Court what this was.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was going to the position marked 5 Bravo. I had other military observers with me. There's a small road that leads to it which looks straight down the hill towards the railway. We usually took a small track to the side of the road, but for some reason I walked down the road. The sniper took his shot. It passed me on my right-hand side, and the shot was from between 6 and 800 metres. I then took cover along the track that I should have been using in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of the road?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was just a track that led to the position. We didn't deal in any road names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: At that time, did you wear anything which was indicative of your position that you were a UN person?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had a blue flack vest and I would have been wearing my blue beret with the white badge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Was that the same outfit your colleagues had?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would have had something similar, but they would all be wearing their own national uniform. And some of them had a flack vest which would be very dark blue, and others would have been wearing a bib with white letters on the front with "UN" written on it. So they all individually were clearly UN personnel, but we were not all dressed exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. In concluding this issue, I would again refer to the last quote I put to you, and I quote it again: "And the fire would come from the south." This referred to the incident when you said there were signs on the corners of the road and so on. Now, when you say "and the fire would come from the south," what was the south, or what was on the south?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the south was rising ground which would lead up to the hills towards Trebevic, so this is the southern area that I was referring to, where the slightly wooded and urban area is indicated on the map, south of Papa headquarters and south of the Presidency, which is up a steep slope.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And which part, which side of the confrontation line was that south?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be coming from the area which -- some of which was no-man's land, so it would be south of the front line as indicated on the map here. This is the front line which I've drawn in black which is only an approximation from my memory. It is from the area here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I understand that. Thanks. And south of this confrontation line was an area controlled by whom?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally by the Serbs, because those areas of no-man's land where there would be wide-open fields, but they were the dominant forces there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. Turning to the next issue of multibarrel rocket launcher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, how much time would you still need? I think perhaps it's better to have the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, Your Honours. I think probably 10 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps we have a break until 5 minutes past 6.00. Mr. Harding, if you could use the 20 minutes to go through your notes, it might give you a more comfortable feeling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Harding, did you have a chance to go through your diary and check whether you could find the date of this shelling incident?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found an entry on the 4th of December when the PTT was shelled. But my writing wasn't exactly brilliant at the time of writing in this diary, and I didn't have enough time to find the specific incident where we timed the flight of the ammunition rounds. But I can clearly remember doing it, because it had only been a short time before I was sent to Bosnia that we had been doing that as part of a British army exercise, and we were controlling the fire. And it is exactly the same. And that's why it's so clear in my mind. But the PTT was shelled on the 4th of December, and I still need more time to go through all of my scribbling, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you are confident that it was after September 1992?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, the second incident you had mentioned today was the incident you were sniped at close to the railway system. Do you recall when that happened, with or without your diary? And I guess if you don't recall, we won't go through the diary exercise again.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been towards the end of September, because I was showing people the observation post. And to be showing them, I had to have time in theatre. So it was definitely in September. The weather was good and it was hot. So that narrows it down to definitely September.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you said end of September.

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within September, because I can distinctly remember I was showing people where it was, and the weather was warm. We would be moving from there shortly, and so that sort of narrows it down to the latter part of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The next issue is the issue of multibarrel rocket launcher, and it's to be found in my records on page 4481. I just have a brief point. You were asked by my learned friend Pilipovic to tell --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So that we can save time, would you please tell me which day you're referring to, because there were two days?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think it's the 8th of December, 1992, as far as I recall because that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I think Mr. Piletta-Zanin is asking for the 25th or the 26th of February if it was during cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes, sorry for that. 26th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see a multibarrel rocket launcher on page 4543, line 22, but I still have to check the context.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the word "Zuc hill area" are also code words to discover where we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The only question I'm asking you about this incident is you answered, and I quote: "The launcher must have been located northwest of Papa 2 because of the straight line. That line goes through where I have written on the map the area of Zuc." Can you tell us by referring to the map where the front line was in the area of Zuc at the time that you had observed the firing?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: By looking at the map, there's the area of Zuc as drawn. And the front line was approximately where the black line has been drawn. And we were at the position here marked with a plus 1 and a number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And do you know more about the position of this rocket system, at least on which side of the confrontation line which you have just referred to was it positioned?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rockets flew directly overhead, which gave us one point. We watched them land to the east of Papa headquarters, which gave us another point. We then did a back bearing and draw the line, and we could then deduce that it came from in the area northwest of our position. We were fairly close to the front line because we were observing shelling. Therefore, the shots must have come from the other side of this hill, which then put it on the Serbian army side. The front line could be seen, because we had just seen shelling on the front line, and it was on the other side. It was northwest.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harding. The next point I want to clarify with you deals with page reference 4458, and the buzz word is "self-propelled artillery." And this is again the 26th of February, 2002. You answered a question by the Defence, and I quote: "At Papa 2, there were self-propelled artillery known as the 2S1, and there was a counterbattery radar mounted on an armoured vehicle which I do not know the designation of. Throughout my time, to the best of my knowledge, these vehicles never moved, and there was no maintenance carried out on them and they were further down the hill from Papa 1." My question to you is, did you ever see any of these weapons firing from Papa 2?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Or are you aware of any reports that any of these weapon systems fired?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an observation post northeast from those guns, and they never reported any firing from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harding. The next issue, and we are coming close to the end, you were asked whether you had -- and this is on page 4458 and 59, you were asked whether you had, and I quote: "Any problems when setting up Papa 6 positions." And the code word is "reconnaissance" in French. The English word, I guess, the same. Your answer was: "Yes, we did. The initial problem was trying to find a location where we could put the observation post. During our initial reconnaissance, we were fired at by 12.7 millimetre machine-gun, and we had to withdraw down the hill." Do you recall in your observation who fired at you?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, I continue quoting you: "We then moved to the west and found the location which eventually became Papa 6. And then all of the grid references for Papa 6 observation posts, I was informed that they were given to the Lima side to give to the Serbian army so that they know exactly where we were. Within 24 hours, every OP had been engaged and fired at by either mortars or artillery, and a round of mortar landed directly on top of the building that we were using as the observation post." Can you tell us who engaged every OP?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't see weapons actually firing but -- and we didn't have any reports of any outgoing firing from any of my observation posts, which by that time covered the majority of the city, and so I would say that it was from the Bosnian Serb army, as they were the only ones that had been given the six-figure grid references, especially of Papa 6 because it was a new location.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harding. The last two questions are as follows, and they originate from comments you made today: You were asked about the functioning of telephone communication at the PTT building. In your recollection, when did the telephone system stop working?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be difficult for me to give a precise date on that, because we were using radios at that time. I would say it would have been the end of August, beginning of September. It's really difficult for me to say because we didn't use the telephones.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And my last question would be, what was the most common car used in Sarajevo while you were there?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: A white Volkswagen Golf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not quite sure of the relevance of this question, and also what part are we talking about with respect to the users?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that, the question has already been answered. Your objection is denied, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. The question as such is not inadmissible. The answer had been given already, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honours. That concludes my cross-examination -- I'm sorry, re-examination. At one time, perhaps now or after you had your questions asked, I would like to formally introduce, tender, the exhibits which come with Mr. Harding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Waespi, I suggest that we'll deal with that when the witness has been led out of the courtroom. But of course, we'll not let the witness go until I've checked whether any of my colleagues or myself still have questions for him. Judge Nieto-Navia has one or more questions to be put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: You have just said that the white Volkswagen Golf was the car which was more commonly used in Sarajevo, and a moment ago, you said that the army used white Volkswagen Golfs as well. My question is: The people in general, the individuals which -- who were not members of the army, used the Volkswagen Golf as well?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Volkswagen Golf seemed to be used by a lot of people and it continually gave us cause for concern, as one of our vehicles was the white Volkswagen Golf and they kept stealing pieces from it. But it was used by a cross-section of the population as well as ourselves. So some people would be met wearing a military jacket, and others would be in complete civilian clothes. We never stopped any of them to identify what they were doing and where they were going. So it was a complete -- I would say it was a cross-section of the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi also has one or more questions to put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My first question relates to the cars, especially the Golf cars that you have seen in quantity. You've seen a lot of them, you said. You also told us that you thought that it was impossible to fire mortars on cars, but that it was possible to mount them on top of vehicles and to carry them and then fire from a position. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The mortar, take it apart, put all the pieces in the car, and then drive somewhere and then take it out and reassemble it outside of the car, and then it could be fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you mean without bringing any modifications to the car?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: By laying down the seats and producing a cargo area, the mortar components themselves are man portable. But you couldn't -- then the mortar would have to be set up on the ground, and then fired and then taken apart again. The mortar concerned, for example, it can be taken apart and troops can parachute with those pieces, which gives you an idea of how large they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the calibre of mortars, according to you, what were they? If we suppose that they were fired from the perimeter of the hospital, can they reach the target? The trajectory Of the mortar, what would it be? If a mortar is fired from within the hospital circle, could it actually achieve or reach the target, to your mind?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mortars in question are 82-millimetre mortars. They have a range of 3 kilometres, which would take them out beyond the front lines when fired to the north from the hospital. So they were very capable of firing into the area held by Bosnian Serb positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I see. So if we understand correctly, you have stated during your cross-examination on the 26th of February that Mount Igman was under Serbian control. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mount Igman was under -- Mount Igman is under Bosnia -- ABiH control, not the Serbian control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And you have stated that the front line would shift in the sense that in that region, it would change places, or during the time you were there, was the Mount Igman always under the control of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mount Igman was always under ABiH control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I have but one last question for you, Witness: I would like to know, what is your definition of "militia"? You told us that there were some differences between militia and paramilitary groups, according to you. The definition is well known in the military jargon, and if I understand correctly, the difference that you see in the two is based on the fact that militia is still under a command, and on the other side, the paramilitary groups are not under the control of a predetermined commander. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And according to you, those who were members of the militia, and in this particular case of the Bosnian militia, were these men militiamen or paramilitary men? Were they under the control of a military authority or are we talking about groups that did not have a unique commandment?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: These militia were under the control of a military authority and they were not working to their own aims and objectives. They were controlled from outside of their battery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harding, since I've no further questions for you, this concludes your, I would say, split-up testimony given in this Court. But I see that Mr. Waespi might be of a different opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, only shortly or for a short while, Your Honours, just two clarifications of points which came out of questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The questions of the Judges. Yes, of course. And if we -- yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] It's a little bit of a never-ending story when things seem so clear. If the Prosecution wishes to start up and open another round of questions, we will stay here and we will listen to this. But we would prefer actually that this does not happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber is of the opinion that of course no new issues can be raised at this very moment, but if it is an issue that has been touched upon by the questions by the Judges, then you're allowed to put these questions. And of course, the story is ending, but not ending before the Defence then has had an opportunity to put additional questions in only this respect to the witness as well. Yes, please, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just a point to clarify about the white Volkswagen Golf cars, you said earlier that some were painted green and by hand, I understand, to identify them as military cars used by the army. Is that what you are saying, or can you tell us how that relates to the white cars still used for whatever purpose and the green repainted cars?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, some had been painted obviously by hand and brush, and I can only presume it's because they were to go near the front line, and it was to tone them down so they would not become an easy target. As to who was driving them, I would presume that it would be the military personnel. But they were very prominent because they were painted by hand rather than spray.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the second point is also for clarification purposes: You talked a lot about militia and the questions asked by the Judges, by Your Honour, also relates to that. For you, was the ABiH, the Bosnian Muslim army, a militia army as a whole or did it have sort of component parts that were militia in the way you defined it? Can you tell us the relationship between the militia and the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to militia, it was the personnel manning the 105-millimetre artillery battery, because -- some had uniforms, some did not. As their training would progress and presumably they got more uniformed, they may well all have the same uniform but they still did not have a large amount of military training. But they are working to a common aim with command from a higher authority. To answer your question, it would be they would get more uniform but they would still in essence be a militia because they haven't had the training. But by looking at them, you wouldn't really be able to tell unless you questioned them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And when you say they were part of the military hierarchy, you mean the ABiH hierarchy with ultimately what you answered Mr. Izetbegovic as the commander in chief?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They had command from a higher authority, and the difference being that a paramilitary would write their own objectives, and if they didn't all agree with it, some of them would then break away as another paramilitary group and work to their own objectives. And there is the difference between a militia and a paramilitary. Paramilitaries work on their own, to their own benefits, whereas a militia is locally recruited civilians given military training as soon as possible, equipped as best they can and work to a common aim.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Waespi. Any need to put additional questions, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, to say what the Prosecution just said a few minutes ago, it's just some points of clarification. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Piletta-Zanin, give you the opportunity to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you have talked earlier about these Golf vehicles that were painted by hand and with a brush. And this was done especially when they were to be sent near the front line, if I understood you correctly, so that they don't become "easy targets." Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a presumption that they were to go near the front line. And if they were to, then it would stop them becoming an easy target, an easily observable target.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do I understand you correctly when I attempt, for instance, to interpret your words with regards to these cars having been artisanal [phoen] paint that basically they were done -- it was not a professional paint job that was done in this case?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, since we do know very well that there wasn't enough fuel in Sarajevo, do you know if the paint was available as well?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the fuel state of the city was. And as regard other supplies, I didn't interact with that side. That would be the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you see paint shops in Sarajevo that were selling paint?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Perhaps that goes beyond the mere issue of clarifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Mr. President, that everything that is very clear may look obscure to the Prosecution, but I do believe that I'm trying to clarify the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was, did you see paint shops in Sarajevo that were selling paint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no, because most of the shops were closed, and I wouldn't know what they were selling because we didn't go into any of the shops, if you can understand. I wouldn't know a paint shop if it was written in a foreign language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further clarifications to be asked, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, just a few, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, is it possible that a large number of these white Golf vehicles that came out of the factory could not have been painted just because, in fact, there weren't enough paint available?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how much paint there was available, so I can't really answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Earlier, you talked about white Golf vehicles in which people in uniform were. Do you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And in fact, can we say that there were more white Golf vehicles than Golf vehicles painted in what is known as camouflage paint?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were referring to the number of Volkswagen Golf vehicles generally, and there were a significant number of them. As to the division between how many were painted in camouflage and how many were not, I couldn't really make a statement because that would depend how many came down or drove through the city when I personally happened to be there.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. And the very last question, Witness: On page 17, line 5 and on the line 6, in answer to a question by the Prosecution with regards to the militia, the question was, Was the militia armed when they were on the front, and you answered yes in general terms. But in order to avoid any confusion and with regards to your last question with regards to militia, I would like to know, Witness, that when you talked about militia, you were talking about all the people and not only all the concerned people by this definition, and not only by some members that you were able to observe on positions Papa 5 and Papa 1?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the term "militia" cannot be applied to everybody because a militia is a locally recruited person who is given training. Therefore, it can't apply to everybody. It would only be those given the training.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I will stop you here. My question was the following: You said what militia is. You said that all the people who are concerned by this definition and not only some people manning artillery weapons that you were able to observe positioned at Papa 1 and Papa 4?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been those people at other parts of the front line that have been locally recruited.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So your last answer given to the Prosecution did not encompass just some workers, some people who were situated at Papa 4 and Papa 1?

utterances.speaker: CARL DANIEL EDWIN HARDING [Resumed]
utterances.text: It encompasses those people at Papa 1 that were manning the artillery. They were not to be considered workers because their job was the artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes. This encompasses them, but it is not exclusively, it is not only these people. Do we agree with this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you, Mr. Harding, see whether I understand the question of Mr. Piletta-Zanin well. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, do you intend to ask the witness whether, apart from the people you saw at Papa 1 and Papa 4 and which fall within his definition of militia that you would find elsewhere members of militia as well? Is that...?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but this is what the witness already stated while giving an answer earlier. But since his very last answer seemed more restrictive, I just wanted to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He wants to know whether you saw people falling within the definition of militia apart from Papa 1 and Papa 4 at other places as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Well, Mr. Harding, I was a bit quick when I said that we concluded already your examination as a witness, and that we still had to deal with the documents. But no more questions for you. Thank you very much more coming, coming twice even, and answering all the questions. I know it has been quite a long time that you have been with us in this courtroom. Thank you very much for answering the questions and thus in assisting both the parties and the Court to perform their tasks. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you guide us through the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, would you please listen very carefully when the Madam Registrar tries to guide us through the papers, since it is already a long time ago and I'd rather not make any mistake. Madam Registrar, what do we have on our list?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P3662, six photographs. Exhibit P3661, UNPROFOR report from squadron leader Harding. P3660, UNPROFOR report, Carl Harding. P3644.CH, map marked by witness. D53, a map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Let me just first ask Mr. Waespi whether all the documents he intended to tender have been mentioned by the registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, there is -- it's correct what the registrar said. This is this after-incident report which is Prosecution Number 3659, which has already been signed by Mr. Harding which was given to us by Mr. Harding at the same time like the two battle-damage assessment reports. And we would also propose to tender -- they were also listed on that letter which we have given.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I do have copies of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I believe that at the time, and in spite of the fact that the Defence had to prepare in a real hurry, we had accepted the photographies, so that everybody can know what we're talking about. But I believe that the question as to the admissibility of reports was a pending question, Mr. President. And I do not remember if you had rendered a decision. I believe that the Defence had said at the time that we do not find it admissible, that in extremis some documents be produced, that the Prosecution is trying to -- had in time or was able to consult for quite a while, and we didn't agree with the fact that we were presented with these documents shortly before the hearing. And we believe that these documents were not communicated to us in due time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, I'll inform the Defence that the registrar just informed me that a full set of colour copies of the photographs are available since, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you raised the issue on whether the objection that you received a copy of the report only shortly before the trial would not change even although the cross-examination of Mr. Harding was resumed approximately one month later. The Chamber prefers to give its final decisions on these issues tomorrow and not today.
